blocks.p: Adam asks about the motions of the heavens, receives an answer that leaves the question open, and is urged to seek instead the things more worth knowing. Adam agrees, and, still wanting to keep Raphael with him, tells him what he remembers since his own creation: how he was placed in Paradise, his talk with God about solitude and fit companionship, and his first meeting and marriage with Eve. He discusses this with the angel, who, after repeating his warnings, departs.

v: The angel ended, and in Adam’s ear
So charming left his voice that he a while
Thought him still speaking, still stood fixed to hear;
Then, as new-waked, he gratefully replied:
“What thanks sufficient, or what recompense
Equal have I to render you, divine
Historian, who so largely have allayed
The thirst I had for knowledge, and vouchsafed
This friendly condescension to relate
Things else unsearchable by me, now heard
With wonder, but delight, and, as is due,
With glory attributed to the high
Creator? Something yet of doubt remains,
Which only your solution can resolve.
When I behold this goodly frame, this world
Of heaven and earth consisting, and compute
Their magnitudes, this earth a spot, a grain,
An atom, with the firmament compared
And all her numbered stars, that seem to roll
Across immeasurable space (for such
Their distance argues, and their swift return
Diurnal) merely to dispense their light
Around this lightless earth, this pinpoint spot,
One day and night, in all their vast survey
Useless besides, I reason and I wonder
How Nature, wise and frugal, could commit
Such disproportions, with superfluous hand
So many nobler bodies to create,
Greater so manifold, for this one use,
For all that shows, and on their orbs impose
Such restless revolution, day by day
Repeated, while the sedentary earth,
That better might with far less compass move,
Served by more noble than herself, attains
Her end without least motion, and receives,
As tribute brought by such a boundless journey
Of incorporeal speed, her warmth and light:
Speed of a swiftness numbers fail to tell.”
So spoke our sire, and by his look he seemed
Lost in abstruse and studious thought; which Eve
Perceiving, where she sat apart in sight,
With lowliness majestic from her seat,
And grace that made beholders wish her stay,
Rose, and went out among her fruits and flowers,
To visit how they prospered, bud and bloom,
Her nursery; they at her coming sprang,
And, touched by her fair care, more gladly grew.
Yet she did not depart as if such talk
Did not delight her, or her ear could not
Take in high things: such pleasure she reserved,
For Adam to relate, she sole to hear;
Her husband as the teller she preferred
Before the angel, and of him to ask
Chose rather; he, she knew, would intermix
Sweet digressions, and would solve high dispute
With conjugal caresses; from his lip
Not words alone pleased her. Oh, when meet now
Such pairs, in love and mutual honor joined?
With goddesslike demeanor out she went,
Not unattended; for on her, as queen,
A train of winning graces always waited,
And from about her shot darts of desire
Into all eyes, to wish her still in sight.
And Raphael now, to Adam’s doubt proposed,
Benevolent and affable, replied:
“To ask or search I blame you not; for heaven
Is as the book of God before you set,
In which to read his wondrous works, and learn
His seasons, hours, or days, or months, or years.
This to attain, if heaven moves or earth
Matters not, if you reckon right; the rest
From man or angel the great Architect
Did wisely to conceal, and not divulge
His secrets to be scanned by those who ought
Rather admire; or, if they wish to try
Conjecture, he his fabric of the heavens
Has left to their disputes, perhaps to move
His laughter at their quaint opinions, wide,
Hereafter, when they come to model heaven
And calculate the stars: how they will wield
The mighty frame, how build, unbuild, contrive
To save appearances, how gird the sphere
With centric and eccentric scribbled over,
Cycle and epicycle, orb in orb.
Already by your reasoning this I guess,
Who are to lead your offspring, and suppose
That bodies bright and greater should not serve
The less, not bright, nor heaven such journeys run,
Earth sitting still, when she alone receives
The benefit. Consider first, that great
Or bright implies not excellence: the earth,
Though, in comparison with heaven, so small,
Nor glittering, may of solid good contain
More plenty than the sun that barren shines,
Whose virtue on itself works no effect,
But in the fruitful earth; there first received,
His beams, inactive else, their vigor find.
Yet not to earth are those bright luminaries
Of service, but to you who dwell on earth.
“And for the heavens’ wide circuit, let it speak
The Maker’s high magnificence, who built
So spacious, and his line stretched out so far,
That man may know he dwells not in his own:
An edifice too large for him to fill,
Lodged in a small partition, and the rest
Ordained for uses to his Lord best known.
The swiftness of those circles attribute,
Though numberless, to his omnipotence,
That to corporeal substances could add
Speed almost spiritual. You think me not slow,
Who since the morning hour set out from Heaven
Where God resides, and by midday arrived
In Eden: distance inexpressible
By numbers that have names. But this I urge,
Admitting motion in the heavens, to show
Invalid all that moved you so to doubt it;
Not that I so affirm, though so it seems
To you who have your dwelling here on earth.
God, to remove his ways from human sense,
Placed heaven so far from earth that earthly sight,
If it presumes, might err in things too high,
And gain no advantage. What if the sun
Is center to the world, and other stars,
By his attractive virtue and their own
Incited, dance about him various rounds?
Their wandering course, now high, now low, then hid,
Progressive, retrograde, or standing still,
In six you see; and what if, seventh to these,
The planet earth, so steadfast though she seems,
Should move, unfelt, in three distinct motions?
Which else to several spheres you must ascribe,
Moved contrary, with crosswise obliquities,
Or save the sun his labor, and that swift
Nocturnal and diurnal rhomb supposed,
Invisible else above all stars, the wheel
Of day and night; which needs not your belief,
If earth, by her own labor, fetches day,
Traveling east, and, with her part turned away
From the sun’s beam, meets night, her other part
Still luminous with his ray. What if that light,
Sent from her through the wide transparent air,
To the terrestrial moon is as a star,
Enlightening her by day, as she by night
This earth? Reciprocal, if land is there,
Fields and inhabitants. Her spots you see
As clouds, and clouds may rain, and rain produce
Fruits in her softened soil, for some to eat
Allotted there; and other suns, perhaps,
With their attendant moons, you will descry,
Communicating male and female light,
Which two great sexes animate the world,
Stored in each orb perhaps with some that live.
For such vast room in nature unpossessed
By living soul, deserted, desolate,
Only to shine, yet scarcely to contribute
Each orb a glimpse of light, conveyed so far
Down to this peopled earth, which then returns
Light back to them, is open to dispute.
“But whether things are thus, or whether not,
Whether the sun, predominant in heaven,
Rise on the earth, or earth rise on the sun,
He from the east begin his flaming road,
Or she from west advance her silent course
With inoffensive pace that, spinning, sleeps
On her soft axle, while she paces even,
And bears you soft with the smooth air along,
Do not disturb your thoughts with hidden things;
Leave them to God above, serve him and fear him.
Of other creatures, as may please him best,
Wherever placed, let him dispose; take joy
In what he gives to you, this Paradise
And your fair Eve; heaven is for you too high
To know what passes there. Be lowly wise:
Think only what concerns you and your being;
Dream not of other worlds, what creatures there
Live, in what state, condition, or degree,
Content with what so far has been revealed
Not of earth only, but of highest Heaven.”
To whom thus Adam, cleared of doubt, replied:
“How fully you have satisfied me, pure
Intelligence of Heaven, angel serene,
And freed from intricacies, taught to live
The easiest way, nor with perplexing thoughts
To interrupt life’s sweetness, from which God
Has bidden all our anxious cares dwell far,
And not molest us, unless we ourselves
Seek them with wandering thoughts and notions vain.
But the mind, or fancy, is apt to rove
Unchecked, and to her roving there’s no end,
Till, warned, or by experience taught, she learns
That not to know at large of things remote
From use, obscure and subtle, but to know
That which before us lies in daily life
Is the prime wisdom; what is more is fume,
Or emptiness, or foolish irrelevance,
And renders us, in things that most concern,
Unpracticed, unprepared, and at a loss.
“Therefore from this high pitch let us descend
A lower flight, and speak of things at hand,
Useful, from which a mention may arise
Of something not unseasonable to ask,
By leave, and with your usual grace allowed.
You I have heard relate what had been done
Before my memory; now hear me tell
My story, which perhaps you have not heard;
And day is not yet spent; till then you see
How subtly to detain you I devise,
Inviting you to hear while I relate,
Foolish, but that I hope for your reply;
For while I sit with you I seem in Heaven,
And sweeter your discourse is to my ear
Than fruits of palm tree, pleasantest to thirst
And hunger both, from labor, at the hour
Of sweet repast; they sate us, and soon fill,
Though pleasant; but your words, with grace divine
Imbued, bring to their sweetness no satiety.”
To whom thus Raphael answered, heavenly meek:
“Nor are your lips ungraceful, sire of men,
Nor tongue ineloquent; for God on you
Abundantly his gifts has also poured,
Inward and outward both, his image fair:
Speaking or mute, all comeliness and grace
Attend you, and form each word, each motion.
Nor less in Heaven we think of you on earth
Than of our fellow servant, and inquire
Gladly into the ways of God with man:
For God, we see, has honored you, and set
On man his equal love: so, please, speak on;
For I that day, as it fell out, was absent,
Bound on a voyage uncharted and obscure,
Far on excursion toward the gates of Hell,
Squared in full legion (such command we had),
To see that none came out from there a spy
Or enemy, while God was at his work,
Lest he, incensed at such a bold eruption,
Destruction with creation might have mixed.
Not that they dared without his leave attempt,
But us he sends upon his high commands
For state, as sovereign King, and so to train
Our prompt obedience. Fast we found, fast shut,
The dismal gates, and barricaded strong;
But long before we neared, we heard within
Noise, other than the sound of dance or song:
Torment, and loud lament, and furious rage.
Glad we returned up to the coasts of light
Before the Sabbath evening: such our charge.
But now your own account; for I attend,
Pleased with your words no less than you with mine.”
So spoke the godlike Power, and thus our sire:
“For man to tell how human life began
Is hard; for who has known his own beginning?
Desire with you still longer to converse
Induced me. As new-waked from soundest sleep,
Soft on the flowery grass I found I lay
In balmy sweat, which with his beams the sun
Soon dried, and on the steaming moisture fed.
Straight toward heaven my wondering eyes I turned,
And gazed a while on the wide sky, till, raised
By quick instinctive motion, up I sprang,
As though I strove to reach it, and upright
Stood on my feet. About me round I saw
Hill, dale, and shady woods, and sunny plains,
And liquid lapse of murmuring streams; by these,
Creatures that lived, and moved, and walked, or flew,
Birds on the branches warbling; all things smiled;
With fragrance and with joy my heart overflowed.
Myself I then examined, limb by limb
Surveyed, and sometimes walked, and sometimes ran
With supple joints, as lively vigor led;
But who I was, or where, or from what cause,
Knew not; I tried to speak, and spoke at once;
My tongue obeyed, and readily could name
All that I saw. ‘O sun,’ I said, ‘fair light,
And you, enlightened earth, so fresh and gay,
You hills and dales, you rivers, woods, and plains,
And you that live and move, fair creatures, tell,
Tell, if you saw, how came I thus, how here?
Not of myself; by some great Maker then,
In goodness and in power preeminent.
Tell me how I may know him, how adore,
From whom I have it that I move and live,
And feel that I am happier than I know.’
“While thus I called, and strayed I knew not where,
From where I first drew air, and first beheld
This happy light, when no answer returned,
On a green shady bank, profuse with flowers,
I sat down, pensive; there a gentle sleep
First found me, and with soft oppression seized
My drowsy sense, untroubled, though I thought
I then was passing to my former state,
Insensible, and about to dissolve;
When suddenly stood at my head a dream,
Whose inward apparition gently moved
My fancy to believe I still had being,
And lived. One came, it seemed, of shape divine,
And said, ‘Your home awaits you, Adam; rise,
First man, of men innumerable ordained
First father: called by you, I come, your guide
To the garden of bliss, your seat prepared.’
“So saying, by the hand he took and raised me,
And over fields and waters, as in air
Smooth gliding, stepless, led me up at last
A wooded mountain, whose high top was level,
A circuit wide, enclosed, with noblest trees
Planted, with walks and bowers, that what I saw
Of earth before seemed scarcely pleasant. Each tree,
Laden with fairest fruit that hung to the eye
Tempting, stirred in me sudden appetite
To pluck and eat; at which I woke, and found
Before my eyes all real, as the dream
Had vividly portrayed. Here had begun
New wanderings, had not he who was my guide
Up to this place appeared among the trees,
Presence divine. Rejoicing, but in awe,
In adoration at his feet I fell
Submissive; he raised me: ‘Whom you sought I am,’
Said mildly, ‘Author of all this you see
Above, or round about you, or beneath.
This Paradise I give you; count it yours
To till and keep, and of the fruit to eat:
Of every tree that in the garden grows
Eat freely with glad heart; fear here no dearth.
But of the tree whose operation brings
Knowledge of good and ill, which I have set
As pledge of your obedience and your faith,
Amid the garden by the Tree of Life,
Remember what I warn you: shun to taste,
And shun the bitter consequence: for know,
The day you eat of it, my sole command
Transgressed, inevitably you shall die;
From that day mortal, and this happy state
You’ll lose, expelled from here into a world
Of woe and sorrow.’ Sternly he pronounced
The rigid prohibition, which resounds
Still dreadful in my ear, though in my choice
Not to incur; but soon his clear aspect
Returned, and gracious purpose thus renewed:
“’Not only these fair bounds, but all the earth
To you and to your race I give; as lords
Possess it, and all things that live therein,
Or live in sea, or air, beast, fish, and fowl.
In sign of which, each bird and beast behold
After their kinds; I bring them to receive
From you their names, and pay you fealty
With low subjection; understand the same
Of fish within their watery residence,
Not summoned here, since they cannot exchange
Their element to draw the thinner air.’
“As thus he spoke, each bird and beast, behold,
Approaching two by two; these cowering low
With blandishment, each bird stooped on his wing.
I named them as they passed, and understood
Their nature, with such knowledge God endowed
My sudden apprehension; but in these
I did not find what I still thought I lacked,
And to the heavenly vision thus presumed:
“’Oh, by what name, for you above all these,
Above mankind, or all above mankind,
Surpass by far my naming, how may I
Adore you, Author of this universe,
And all this good to man, for whose well-being
So amply, and with hands so liberal,
You have provided all things? But with me
I see no one to share. In solitude
What happiness? Who can enjoy alone,
Or, all enjoying, what contentment find?’
“Thus I, presumptuous; and the vision bright,
As with a smile more brightened, thus replied:
“’You call this solitude? Is not the earth
With various living creatures, and the air,
Replenished, and all these at your command
To come and play before you? Do you not know
Their language and their ways? They also know,
And reason not contemptibly; with these
Find pastime, and bear rule; your realm is large.’
“So spoke the universal Lord, and seemed
So ordering. I, with leave of speech implored,
And humble supplication, thus replied:
“’Let not my words offend you, heavenly Power,
My Maker; be propitious while I speak.
Have you not made me here your substitute,
And set these lesser beings far below me?
Among unequals what society
Can suit, what harmony or true delight?
Which must be mutual, in proportion due
Given and received; but in disparity,
The one intense, the other always slack,
Cannot well suit with either, but soon prove
Tedious alike. Of fellowship I speak
Such as I seek, fit to participate
All rational delight, wherein the brute
Cannot be human consort; they rejoice
Each with their kind, lion with lioness;
So fitly you have joined them all in pairs;
Much less can bird with beast, or fish with fowl,
So well converse, nor with the ox the ape;
Worse then can man with beast, and least of all.’
“To which the Almighty answered, not displeased:
“’A choice and subtle happiness, I see,
You set before yourself here, in the choice
Of your companions, Adam, and will taste
No pleasure, though in pleasure, solitary.
What do you think then of me, and my state?
Do I seem to you sufficiently possessed
Of happiness, or not? who am alone
From all eternity, for none I know
Second to me or like, much less my equal.
How then have I with whom to hold converse,
Except the creatures which I made, and those
To me inferior, infinite descents
Beneath what other creatures are to you?’
“He ceased; I humbly answered: ‘To attain
The height and depth of your eternal ways
All human thoughts fall short, Supreme of things!
You in yourself are perfect, and in you
No lack is to be found; not so is man,
But in degree, the cause of his desire
By fellowship with his own like to help
Or solace his defects. No need that you
Should propagate, already infinite,
And through all numbers absolute, though One;
But man by number is to manifest
His single imperfection, and beget
Like of his like, his image multiplied,
In unity defective, which requires
Collateral love, and dearest amity.
You, in your secrecy, although alone,
Best with yourself accompanied, seek not
Social communication; yet, so pleased,
Can raise your creature to what height you will
Of union or communion, deified;
I, by conversing, cannot these erect
From prone, nor in their ways find any joy.’
“Thus I, emboldened, spoke, and freedom used
Permitted, and acceptance found, which gained
This answer from the gracious voice divine:
“’Thus far to test you, Adam, I was pleased,
And find you knowing not of beasts alone,
Which you have rightly named, but of yourself,
Expressing well the spirit within you free,
My image, not imparted to the brute,
Whose fellowship, therefore, unfit for you,
You had good reason freely to dislike,
And keep that mind; for I, before you spoke,
Knew it not good for man to be alone,
And no such company as then you saw
Intended for you, brought for trial only,
To see how you could judge of fit and meet.
What next I bring will please you, be assured:
Your likeness, your fit help, your other self,
Your wish, exactly to your heart’s desire.’
“He ended, or I heard no more; for now
My earthly part, by heavenly overpowered,
Which it had long stood under, strained to the height
In that celestial colloquy sublime,
As with an object that excels the sense,
Dazzled and spent, sank down, and sought repair
In sleep, which instantly fell on me, called
By nature as an aid, and closed my eyes.
My eyes he closed, but left open the cell
Of fancy, my internal sight, by which,
Rapt, as if in a trance, I seemed to see,
Though sleeping, where I lay, and saw the shape,
Still glorious, before whom awake I stood;
Who, stooping, opened my left side, and took
From there a rib, with cordial spirits warm,
And lifeblood streaming fresh; wide was the wound,
But suddenly with flesh filled up and healed.
The rib he formed and fashioned with his hands;
Under his forming hands a creature grew,
Manlike, but different sex, so lovely fair
That what seemed fair in all the world seemed now
Mean, or in her summed up, in her contained
And in her looks, which from that time infused
Sweetness into my heart, unfelt before,
And into all things from her air inspired
The spirit of love and amorous delight.
“She disappeared, and left me dark. I woke
To find her, or forever to deplore
Her loss, and every other joy abjure:
When, out of hope, behold her, not far off,
Such as I saw her in my dream, adorned
With what all earth or heaven could bestow
To make her lovable: and on she came,
Led by her heavenly Maker, though unseen,
And guided by his voice, nor uninformed
Of nuptial sanctity and marriage rites:
Grace was in all her steps, Heaven in her eye,
In every gesture dignity and love.
Overjoyed, I could not hold back, but cried:
‘This turn has made amends; you have fulfilled
Your words, Creator bounteous and benign,
Giver of all things fair, but fairest this
Of all your gifts, nor grudging. Now I see
Bone of my bone, flesh of my flesh, my self
Before me; Woman is her name, of Man
Extracted; for this cause he shall forgo
Father and mother, and to his wife adhere;
And they shall be one flesh, one heart, one soul.’
“She heard me thus; and though divinely brought,
Yet innocence and virgin modesty,
Her virtue, and the knowledge of her worth,
That would be wooed, and not unsought be won,
Not forward, not obtrusive, but retired,
The more desirable; or, to say all,
Nature herself, though pure of sinful thought,
Worked in her so that, seeing me, she turned.
I followed her; she knew what honor was,
And with a yielding majesty approved
My pleaded reason. To the nuptial bower
I led her, blushing like the morn; all Heaven,
And happy constellations, at that hour
Shed down their choicest influence; the earth
Gave sign of joyful greeting, and each hill;
Joyous the birds; fresh breezes and soft airs
Whispered it to the woods, and from their wings
Flung rose, flung fragrance from the spicy shrub,
At play, until the amorous bird of night
Sang nuptial songs, and bade the evening star
Speed to his hilltop, light the bridal lamp.
“Thus I have told you all my state, and brought
My story to the sum of earthly bliss
Which I enjoy, and must confess I find
In all things else delight indeed, but such
As, used or not, works in the mind no change,
Nor vehement desire: these delicacies
I mean of taste, sight, smell, herbs, fruits, and flowers,
Walks, and the melody of birds; but here
Far otherwise: transported I behold,
Transported touch; here passion first I felt,
Commotion strange; in all enjoyments else
Superior and unmoved, here only weak
Against the charm of beauty’s powerful glance.
Or Nature failed in me, and left some part
Not proof enough to withstand such a sight,
Or, from my side subtracting, took perhaps
More than enough; at least on her bestowed
Too much of ornament, in outward show
Elaborate, of inward less exact.
For well I understand, in the prime end
Of nature she is lesser, in the mind
And inward faculties, which most excel;
In outward form, too, she resembles less
His image who made both, and less expresses
The character of that dominion given
Over the creatures; yet when I approach
Her loveliness, so absolute she seems
And in herself complete, so well to know
Her own, that what she wills to do or say
Seems wisest, most virtuous, most discreet, best.
All higher knowledge in her presence falls
Degraded; wisdom in discourse with her
Loses, abashed, and seems like foolishness;
Authority and reason on her wait,
As one intended first, not after made
Incidentally; and, to perfect all,
Greatness of mind and nobleness their seat
Build in her loveliest, and create an awe
About her, like a guard angelic placed.”
To whom the angel, with contracted brow:
“Do not blame Nature; she has done her part;
Do only yours, and do not lose your trust
In Wisdom; she deserts you not, if you
Do not dismiss her when you need her near,
By attributing overmuch to things
Less excellent, as you yourself perceive.
For what do you admire, what transports you so?
An outside? Fair, no doubt, and worthy well
Of cherishing, of honor, and of love,
Not your subjection. Weigh yourself with her;
Then value. Often nothing profits more
Than self-esteem, grounded on just and right,
Well managed; of that skill the more you know,
The more she will acknowledge you her head,
And to realities yield all her shows;
Made so adorned for your delight the more,
So stately, that with honor you may love
Your mate, who sees when you are seen least wise.
But if the sense of touch, by which mankind
Is propagated, seem such dear delight
Beyond all other, think the same is granted
To cattle and each beast; which would not be
To them made common and widespread, if what
Is there enjoyed were worthy to subdue
The soul of man, or passion in him move.
What higher in her company you find
Attractive, human, rational, love still;
In loving you do well, in passion not,
In which true love consists not; love refines
The thoughts, and heart enlarges, has its seat
In reason, and is judicious, is the scale
By which to heavenly love you may ascend,
Not sunk in carnal pleasure; for which cause
Among the beasts no mate for you was found.”
To whom thus Adam, half abashed, replied:
“Neither her outward form, so fair, nor that
In procreation shared by every kind
(Though of the marriage bed I think far higher,
And hold it in mysterious reverence)
So much delights me as those graceful acts,
Those thousand decencies that daily flow
From all her words and actions, mixed with love
And sweet compliance, which declare unfeigned
Union of mind, or in us both one soul;
Harmony to behold in wedded pair
More pleasing than harmonious sound to the ear.
Yet these subject me not; I show to you
What I feel inwardly, yet am not foiled,
Who meet with various objects, from the sense
Variously representing; yet, still free,
Approve the best, and follow what I approve.
You blame me not for love; for love, you say,
Leads up to Heaven, is both the way and guide;
Bear with me, then, if what I ask is lawful:
Do heavenly spirits love? And how do they
Express their love: by looks alone, or mix
Irradiance, virtual or immediate touch?”
To whom the angel, with a smile that glowed
Celestial rosy red, love’s proper hue,
Answered: “Let it suffice you that you know
Us happy, and without love no happiness.
Whatever pure you in the body taste
(And pure you were created) we enjoy
In eminence, and find no obstacle
Of membrane, joint, or limb, exclusive bars;
Easier than air with air, if spirits embrace,
Total they mix, union of pure with pure
Desiring; nor need hampered conveyance,
As flesh to mix with flesh, or soul with soul.
“But I may stay no more; the parting sun
Beyond the earth’s green cape and verdant isles
Hesperian sets, my signal to depart.
Be strong, live happy, and love, but first of all
Him whom to love is to obey, and keep
His great command; take heed lest passion sway
Your judgment to do what free will, untouched,
Would not admit; your own and all your sons’
Welfare or woe is placed in you; beware.
I in your perseverance will rejoice,
And all in bliss: stand fast; to stand or fall
Is free, and in your own decision lies.
Perfect within, require no outward aid,
And all temptation to transgress repel.”
So saying, he arose; whom Adam thus
Followed with benediction: “Since we part,
Go, heavenly guest, ethereal messenger,
Sent from the sovereign goodness I adore.
Gentle to me and affable has been
Your condescension, and shall be honored ever
With grateful memory. And to mankind
Be good and friendly still, and come back often.”
They parted so, the angel up to Heaven
From the thick shade, and Adam to his bower.

blocks.p: The angel ended (1–4). Milton added lines 1–3 and recast line 4 in 1674, when he divided the seventh book of the ten-book first edition into Books VII and VIII.
Historian (7). Raphael, who has narrated the war in Heaven and the six days of creation (Books V–VII).
Diurnal (22). Daily; in the old astronomy the whole heavens wheeled around the earth once every twenty-four hours.
sedentary earth (32). The earth at rest at the center of the universe, as in the Ptolemaic system.
the book of God (67). Nature read as God’s second book beside Scripture [Ps. 19:1]; the heavenly lights mark “seasons, and days, and years” [Gen. 1:14].
save appearances (82). The astronomers’ phrase for devising a model that fits the observed motions, whether or not it is true.
centric and eccentric, cycle and epicycle (83–84). Ptolemaic devices: orbits centered on the earth or off it, and small circles carried on larger ones.
his line stretched out (102). The builder’s measuring line [Job 38:5].
What if the sun is center (122–125). The Copernican hypothesis; Raphael raises it, with the planets drawn by an “attractive virtue,” without deciding between the systems.
In six you see (128). The six “wandering stars” known besides the sun: the moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.
three distinct motions (130). Copernicus gave the earth a daily rotation, a yearly orbit, and a third motion to account for the tilt of its axis.
rhomb (134). The primum mobile, the outermost sphere, imagined as a wheel turning all the heavens once a day.
male and female light (150). The original light of suns and the reflected light of moons.
fume (194). Vapor, smoke: something insubstantial.
fellow servant (225). The angel’s term for himself in Revelation [Rev. 19:10; 22:9].
the gates of Hell (231). Raphael’s guard duty on the day Man was made is Milton’s invention.
Sabbath evening (246). The close of the sixth day, as the seventh, God’s day of rest, began [Gen. 2:2].
Whom you sought I am (316). An echo of God’s name, “I AM,” revealed to Moses [Exod. 3:14].
To till and keep (320). God’s charge to Adam, with the one prohibition [Gen. 2:15–17].
their names (344). Adam’s naming of the animals [Gen. 2:19–20].
substitute (381). Deputy, one who rules in another’s place.
through all numbers absolute, though One (421). God, though one, is complete in himself and needs no other to make him whole.
Collateral (426). Side by side; love between equals rather than between higher and lower.
not good for man to be alone (445). [Gen. 2:18]; “fit help” (450) renders the “help meet for him” of the same verse.
cordial spirits (466). The vital spirits, thought to be made in the heart and carried in the blood.
Bone of my bone (495–499). Adam’s words over Eve; “Woman,” Hebrew ishshah, is taken from “Man,” ish [Gen. 2:23–24].
influence (513). The power once believed to flow from the stars and shape events on earth.
bird of night (518). The nightingale.
the evening star (519). Hesperus, the planet Venus at dusk, which in classical wedding songs signals the bride’s coming.
proof (535). Able to withstand, as armor is proof against a blow.
her head (574). The husband’s headship as Paul describes it [1 Cor. 11:3; Eph. 5:23].
scale (591). Ladder; the Platonic ascent from earthly to heavenly love.
decencies (601). Fitting and gracious ways of acting.
virtual or immediate touch (617). Contact by influence at a distance, or by direct touch.
love’s proper hue (619). Rosy red, the color of love, and of the seraphim, the angels of love.
green cape and verdant isles (631). Cape Verde and the Cape Verde Islands off West Africa; “Hesperian” means western.
Him whom to love is to obey (634). [John 14:15].
